item.title: Radiolab: There and Back Again
item.description:
Today we revisit an episode first aired in 2019. In it we ask a question: When an animal disappears in the winter, where does it go? Oddly enough, this question completely stumped European scientists for thousands of years. And even today, the more we learn about the comings and goings of the animals, the deeper the mystery seems to get. We visit a Bavarian farm with an 11 year old, follow warblers and wildebeests around the world, and get a totally new kind of view of the pulsing flow of animals across the globe.  

LATERAL CUTS:
Have kids? Or, are you just one at heart? Do any of those kids want to know more about Monarchs? Check out a whole episode from our sister program, Terrestrials.

item.title: Freakonomics Radio: 695. Can the U.S. Close Its Fertility Gap?
item.description:
Americans are having fewer children than they want. Government attempts to boost birth rates haven’t done much. But new research points to a surprisingly simple way to help — and it starts at home. (Part one of a two-part series.) 

 

  • SOURCES:
    • Nick Bloom, professor of economics at Stanford University.
    • Melissa Kearney, professor of economics at the University of Notre Dame.
    • Lyman Stone, director of the Pronatalism Initiative at the Institute for Family Studies.

 

  • RESOURCES:
    • "Does Remote Work Increase Fertility?" by Andrew C. Johnston (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2026).
    • "Is the iPhone Birth Control? Causal Evidence from AT&T’s 2007–2011 Carrier Monopoly," by Caitlin K. Meyers and Ezekiel Hooper (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2026).
    • "Work from Home and Fertility," by Steven J. Davis, Cevat Giray Aksoy, Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom, Katelyn Cranney, Mathias Dolls, and Pablo Zarate (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2026).
    • "Why is Fertility so Low in High Income Countries?" by Melissa Schettini Kearney and Phillip B. Levine

item.title: Ignited: Striking Industrial Automation Conversations: The Talent Gap: How the Industrial Automation Industry Finds Its Next Generation of Engineers
item.description:
This episode addresses one of the most pressing challenges in digital transformation and industrial automation: the critical shortage of skilled controls and SCADA engineers. Recorded live at the Ignition Community Conference (ICC) 2026, hosts Travis and Tom discuss what is driving this workforce gap, what it costs integrators and end users when positions remain unfilled, and how the pipeline of new engineering talent can be strengthened. The conversation also highlights the launch of Cognify Connect, a purpose-built platform designed to connect Ignition-certified engineers directly with the organizations that need them.

 

Guest: Kianni Brown

item.title: The Automation Ladies: Beyond Defect Detection: How Overview AI Is Transforming Machine Vision with Russell Nibbelink
item.description:
AI machine vision has been “almost ready” for a long time, but factory teams do not get paid for hype. They get paid for fewer defects, less scrap, higher yield, and systems that actually survive real production. I sit down with Russell, co-founder of Overview AI, to talk about what finally feels different and why their approach stood out to me after years around industrial automation and machine vision.

We dig into the unglamorous truth: vision succeeds or fails on installation details like lighting, lensing, part presentation, and integration. Russell shares how Overview AI brings self-driving style AI into a controlled factory environment, then makes the first deployment easier through customer success support and self-service tools. We also talk about the buying side, including transparent pricing and why they moved away from SaaS subscriptions toward a one-time purchase model that matches CapEx budgets and helps plants justify ROI quickly.

Then we get into the big unlock: generative AI and synthetic data generation for defect detection. Instead of waiting for rare bad parts, teams can generate realistic scratches, dents, bubbles, or missing components to train models and, just as important, to validate inspection coverage before turning on automated rejects. From there, we zoom out to manufacturing intelligence: dashboards and HMI-friendly views that turn inspection results into Pareto charts, shift trends, and continuous improvement signals that cut waste and boost throughput. We also touch on safety-critical use cases, upcoming anomaly detection for PCBA, and what an “onboard agent” could mean for integrators and distributors.

If you care about factory quality inspection, AI vision systems, scrap reduction, and faster time to value in industrial automation, you’ll get a lot from this conversation. item.title: Song Exploder: Mastodon - Your Ghost Again
item.description:
The band Mastodon formed in 2000 in Atlanta, Georgia. They’ve won a Grammy and been nominated for 5 others, and three of their albums have debuted at #1 on Billboard’s Hard Rock charts. For most of their history, they were a four piece, made up of Brann Dailor, Troy Sanders, Bill Kelliher, and Brent Hinds. But in March 2025, Brent Hinds left the band. And later that year, he died in a motorcycle accident. For this episode, I spoke to Brann, Troy, and Bill about making the song “Your Ghost Again,” which came together in the wake of Brent’s death, and the death of Brann’s mother. Along with their new members, Nick Johnston and João Nogueira, they released their 9th album, Marrow Deep, in August 2026. I went to their studio in Atlanta, and talked to them about everything they went through and everything that went into the song “Your Ghost Again.” 

For more info, visit songexploder.net/mastodon.

item.title: What We Spend: I Was Never Going To Be Able To Retire Anyway
item.description: Stephanie is a 61-year-old rideshare driver. She lives with a roommate in the same apartment complex where she grew up. She has little in savings and limited financial wiggle room, but she values the freedom of her work over the stability of a 9-to-5 job. We follow Stephanie as she tries to live by her motto: don’t live to work, work to live.

item.title: Manufacturing Happy Hour: 310: The Automation Skills Gap: Why Manufacturers Need to Train the Workforce They Already Have
item.description:
Five years ago, many companies treated training as optional. That’s changing.

Joining Chris is Christelle Keefer, Director of Training and Certification at the Association for Advancing Automation (A3), back for a second visit. Before she started at A3, she spent years at a robotics OEM working with schools, instructors, and customers worldwide. And if she had her way, this conversation would be happening at a punk rock show.

They discuss what automation training should include and what certifications look like for different roles. Christelle also talks about how manufacturers can prepare the existing workforce for new opportunities, and how educators can help students connect with automation.

In this episode, find out:

  • How stackable credentials let working adults build their skills without taking years away from work
  • Why hands-on equipment time and simulation still matter as more training moves online
  • How manufacturers can upskill the workers they already have, and why tying training to a pay increase or promotion matters
  • How colleges work with local employers to shape their programs, and where apprenticeships fit into the picture
  • What A3 is doing to connect students with manufacturing through competitions, mentorship and the Education Pavilion at Automate
  • What Christelle hopes the future of automation will look like, and why she sees a national strategy as part of the picture

Tweetable Quotes:

item.title: Where Should We Begin? with Esther Perel: I'll Still Be Your Financial Partner, But I'm Done Being Your Wife
item.description:
After a nearly forty-year relationship, they've decided to split. But given the many laws in America that favor married couples, they've decided to try an unconventional arrangement: living 300 miles apart but remaining legally married. They come to Esther wondering how, after decades of emotional enmeshment, they can disentangle their romantic connection while continuing to function like business partners. Esther helps them move into their next phase of life by coaching them past long-held relational patterns so that they can instead offer each other gratitude, regret, and distance.
Producer’s Note: When our anonymous guests do a session with Esther for the podcast, it is an act of generosity for everyone who listens. These sessions are meant not only to support the people in the room with Esther, but all of us who learn from their stories. Our stories have many chapters, and what you hear is just one moment in someone’s journey. So even though the sessions are anonymous, please remember that real people are behind them and they may be reading your comments.
Relationships are undergoing a massive cultural shift. We've never been more connected, and we've never felt more disconnected. We crave understanding and collective experience. We want to be seen but we're optimizing for isolation. Esther believes that the only way to improve our relationships is to remember the basics of being together. This is why she's inviting you to join her for an immersive experience: her international tour, Strangers, Friends, and Lovers. Tickets are selling fast. Get yours now at estherperel.com/tour.

item.title: NerdWallet's Smart Money Podcast: Vicki Gunvalson, Real Housewife on Life Insurance, Lifestyle Creep and Building Wealth
item.description:
Learn how a reality TV star built a career in insurance and why she saves her Hollywood paychecks instead of spending them.
How did an original Real Housewife build a career in finance long before reality TV? Hosts Sean Pyles, CFP®, and Elizabeth Ayoola talk with Vicki Gunvalson, founder of Coto Insurance & Financial Services and an original cast member of The Real Housewives of Orange County. They hear her story about starting over financially after a divorce at 28, how her father’s Alzheimer’s diagnosis and lack of long-term care insurance shaped her career, and the life insurance mistakes she sees most often. You’ll also hear why so many people tune out when insurance comes up, what it takes to go from earning money to building wealth, and why getting your financial documents organized could spare your family a mess later on.
Then, what happens when the reality TV paychecks start rolling in? Vicki explains how she handles her show income, why she kept running her business while filming, and the money habits she’s noticed among her castmates. She also shares her best and worst money moves, her take on renting versus buying a home, and how she earns credit card rewards without carrying a balance. Then Sean and Elizabeth discuss whether they’d ever join a reality show, how a side hustle could boost your savings, and when a little lifestyle creep might be OK.

item.title: This American Life: 901: Is Your Blue My Blue?
item.description:
The doomed project of trying to translate what’s in your head into someone else’s head.

Start a Life Partners free trial to watch our new video, A Night of Stories and Improv.

(00:00:00) Prologue: A while back, Ira woke up with double vision and learned that he had cataracts. After his cataract surgery, he realized the color blue looked very different to him. Now he always wonders: does everyone see the same blue as I do, or is their blue different? (3 minutes)

(00:03:26) Act One: Shaun Bengson has known since he was a kid that he’d very likely lose his hearing as he got older and develop tinnitus. And even after it started, he didn’t do the sensible things that would slow its progression. Shaun and his wife, Abigail, discuss their decisions — and non-decisions — with Ira. And Shaun plays a simulation of what the world now sounds like to him. (27 minutes)

(00:32:50) Act Two: Cluster headaches are sometimes called the most painful medical condition. Researchers who study them wanted to know if that was actually true. They asked cluster patients to compare their headaches to other famously painful conditions. Producer Ike Sriskandarajah, who gets these headaches, was excited to read the findings. But should he tell his pregnant wife? (14 minutes)

(00:46:35) Act Three: Molly’s mom died suddenly last fall, and it flipped the axis of her world. But one day, a friend told her about a special object that really helped him cope with his own father’s death. Molly decides to track this object down. (8 minutes)
